newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia, Croatia protest over authoritarian rule.
newsitem.headline: Serbia, Croatia protest over authoritarian rule.

text.p: Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Franjo Tudjman of Croatia, twin driving forces behind the destruction of former Yugoslavia, are both struggling to stifle outbursts of public discontent with their authoritarian rule.

Huge demonstrations against apparent abuses of power have been staged in Belgrade and Zagreb this month by opposition supporters determined to flaunt discontents that normally simmer below the surface of political life.

An attempt by Croatia's nationalist government to close down Radio 101, a symbol of free speech to many Croats, mobilised 100,000 protesters in Zagreb's biggest demonstration since independence in 1991.

The catalyst in Serbia was President Milosevic's blatant quashing of an opposition victory in municipal elections that would have turfed his ruling socialists out of power in the capital and big industrial cities.
Up to 150,000 angry opposition supporters marched in Belgrade in the strongest challenge to Milosevic since 1991, when he used tanks to quell tumult in the streets.
President Tudjman was out of the country when his ruling HDZ party tried to suppress the radio and was reported to have ordered the opposition to be mollified before his return.

But political sources in both capitals said the message for the two leaders was the same -- weariness with the claims of Serbia's socialists and 74-year-old Tudjman's right-wing HDZ to permanent power, wielded arbitrarily.
The presidents and their parties grew out of the old communist system that kept ex-Yugoslavia in a bureaucratic straitjacket, and there has been no discernible change of ethos.

In contrast with Serbia, Croatia has liberalised its economy but its claimed eagerness to swim in the European mainstream is contradicted by its attachment to illiberal Balkan traditions of political control.
Tudjman and Milosevic both believe in keeping the press on a tight leash, hence the outcry over the future of Radio 101, which a U.S. diplomat in Zagreb called a test case for Croatian democracy.
"Croatia is at a crossroads," he warned. "The government and the people believe they are part of the West. But to be part of the West, you must behave like the West."

Tudjman's government agreed to reconsider the Radio 101 decision but the president told his people: "We will not allow solutions to be imposed from outside... from countries unable to solve their own problems."
The radio dispute followed opposition anger over Tudjman's refusal to recognise their decisive victory in Zagreb municipal elections last year and appoint a non-HDZ mayor.

He is heading into presidential, municipal and regional elections next year with support for the HDZ crumbling under the perception that its leader is an anachronistic autocrat and the party is corrupt.
A growing number of voters question the HDZ's contention that leading Croatia to independence gave it a right to rule and that opposition equals ingratitude.
Tudjman's standing was badly damaged last week while he was in Washington for medical checks. U.S. sources leaked that he was seriously ill with stomach cancer and had only a year to live.
Croatian officials denied the claim and said he suffered from digestive problems, but independent Croatian newspapers also reported they were told he had cancer, but of the prostate.

Political sources said the U.S. version of his illness was a clear prompt to Croatians to start contemplating a future without their ailing president, although he is certain to run for re-election if he is physically able.
Serbian opposition leaders told the country that the government's annulment of the municipal election results was the final proof Milosevic could never be defeated at the ballot box.
With the demonstrations in Belgrade growing, both sides have warned of the danger of the dispute becoming violent.

Western analysts in Belgrade describe Milosevic's socialists as basically the old communist elite recycled under more user-friendly camouflage. There has been no sign that they intend to relinquish either political power or control of the state-dominated economy.
Serbia's problems mirror many of those in Croatia, with the difference that Milosevic, in power for nine years and still only 55, appears determined to remain at the helm well into the next century.
